regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 56.5","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI Composite at 56.5 look unambiguous — until you note that core sector growth decelerated to 4.8% YoY even as IIP capital goods surged 16.9% YoY. The divergence is structural: services and investment are pulling the headline; the goods economy, which employs the informal majority, is not keeping pace. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity is the one number that validates the investment story — above the 75% threshold where private capex historically accelerates.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 6.09% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 6.09% YoY has now breached the RBI's 6% upper tolerance band for three consecutive months (4.45%→5.54%→6.09%), with fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY — a 95th-percentile print — doing the damage. Core CPI at 4.5% YoY is rising but not alarming; the real problem is that food at 8.94% YoY and fuel together are compressing real rural incomes. The inversion: if the RBI holds rates while food and fuel inflation run hot, it is effectively tightening real rates for the urban salaried class while doing nothing to address supply-side price pressures.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.54% YoY; CD ratio 82%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.54% YoY against deposit growth of 16.86% YoY — a 268 bps gap widening for three consecutive months — has pushed the CD ratio to 82%, at the 75th percentile of its 10-year range. Services credit at 28.3% YoY (rising three months straight: 21.4%→22.9%→24.3%→28.3%) is the fastest-growing segment, which means the funding stress is concentrated in the segment least able to access retail deposits. The last time the CD ratio sustained above 80% during a rate pause, the regulator responded with macro-prudential tightening on risk weights — the incentive to act is identical today.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is unchanged, but the policy calculus is deteriorating: CPI has now breached the upper tolerance band, the RBI's own inflation forecast has been revised up to 5.1% YoY, and the Fed is hiking again (3.88% p.a., up three months running). The real repo rate — repo minus headline CPI — is now negative at -84 bps, which means the RBI is inadvertently accommodative even on pause. A rate cut is off the table; the question is whether the next move is a hike, and the fuel inflation trajectory will answer it within two quarters.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (up from 16.1% prior month) and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6%) — both rising for two consecutive months — confirm the investment upcycle is not a statistical artefact. Commercial vehicle sales at 37.6% YoY (up from 12.6% three months ago) corroborate: goods movement is expanding, which means the capex is translating into real economic activity, not just order books. The risk: if the CD ratio forces banks to slow credit growth, the vehicle and equipment financing that underpins this cycle gets squeezed first.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹231290 cr/mo; PV 32.1% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,31,290 cr / month is a 90th-percentile print, but the composition matters: passenger vehicle sales at 32.1% YoY and two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY suggest the surge is broad-based across urban discretionary and rural mobility. The inversion: GST records can reflect formalisation reclassifying existing spend, not new demand — the 23% month-on-month jump from ₹1,88,125 cr warrants triangulation against e-way bill volumes before declaring a demand surge. Household debt at 47.8% of GDP (up from 45.5%) is the quiet constraint: consumption is being partially debt-funded, and at 6.09% YoY CPI, real wage growth for the bottom half is negative.","badge_label":"Demand Surge","badge_type":"b-exp"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.54% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 16.86% YoY — a 268 bps divergence widening for three consecutive months (13.8%→17.1%→19.4%→19.54% credit; 10.8%→17.8%→16.86% deposits). CD ratio now 82% credit ÷ deposits, up from 81% prior month, at 75th percentile of 10-year range. Services credit surging 28.3% YoY (21.4%→22.9%→24.3%→28.3% over three months) — the fastest segment. Agriculture credit at 19.5% YoY, also accelerating. NBFC credit growth at 15.4% YoY, down from 15.8% prior month but still elevated.","implication":"Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% — they will poach deposits from smaller lenders. Avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities; funding costs will rise. Watch for RBI to signal deposit-friendly measures (higher savings rates, CRR cuts) within 2-3 months if divergence persists. Corporate bond issuance at ₹134,000 cr / month (up from ₹18,700 cr / month prior) signals firms are already hedging credit availability by tapping bond markets — a leading indicator of tightening.","pct_10y":75,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 75th percentile historically preceded either RBI rate cuts (to ease deposit pressure) or tighter credit growth. The last time CD ratio was this elevated (2021-22), RBI eventually cut rates and tightened liquidity.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadens Across Sectors","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (prev 16.1%), capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (prev 75.6%), both rising for two consecutive months. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (down from 5% prior month) — a deceleration, but this is noise; the lead indicators (capex goods and utilisation) are accelerating. Services credit at 28.3% YoY (rising three months straight: 21.4%→22.9%→24.3%→28.3%) and agriculture credit at 19.5% YoY (rising three months: 16.8%→17%→17.2%→19.5%) both signal broad-based investment demand. Vehicle credit at 18.8% YoY (up from 15.2% three months ago), commercial vehicle sales at 37.6% YoY (up from 12.6% three months ago).","implication":"Overweight capital goods manufacturers, cement, and steel. Increase exposure to project-linked equities (EPC, infrastructure). Reduce defensives — capex upcycles typically compress multiples on low-growth sectors. Monitor order books for private capex (vs public) — if private capex is driving the cycle, it's more durable. The 77.4% capacity utilisation is still below the 80%+ threshold that typically triggers aggressive capex, so runway remains.","pct_10y":68,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is at 68th percentile; historically, sustained capex cycles begin when utilisation crosses 75% and accelerate above 80%. This is early-to-mid cycle.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Inflows Hit 94th Percentile, But Growth Slowing","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,160 cr / month (latest), down marginally from ₹32,490 cr / month prior month, but at 94th percentile of 10-year range. SIP YoY growth at 8.9% (down from 15% four months ago, 19.85% five months ago) — a sharp deceleration. However, SIP AUM at ₹17.68 lakh cr (up from ₹16.64 lakh cr five months ago), growing faster than SIP account growth (10 mn accounts, down from 10.45 mn five months ago). MF AUM at ₹83.39 lakh cr (at 86th percentile), up from ₹82.03 lakh cr five months ago. Equity MF net inflows at ₹32,994 cr / month (down from ₹38,307 cr / month prior month).","implication":"SIP inflows remain structurally strong but growth is decelerating — a yellow flag for retail sentiment. The divergence between SIP AUM growth (rising) and SIP account growth (flat/declining) suggests affluent money is entering, not mass retail. This is late-cycle behaviour. Maintain overweight on large-cap, dividend-paying equities; reduce small-cap exposure. Monitor SIP growth rate — if it falls below 5% YoY, it signals retail exhaustion.","pct_10y":94,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 94th percentile are historically associated with market peaks or late-cycle euphoria. The last time inflows were this high (2021), they preceded a 20%+ correction.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI's Comfort Zone","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (prev 20.05%), up from 20.05% prior month — a 288 bps jump in one month. This is at 95th percentile of 10-year range. Headline CPI at 6.09% YoY (prev 5.54%), rising for three consecutive months (4.45%→5.54%→6.09%). Food inflation at 8.94% YoY (prev 7.74%), also rising three months straight (5.52%→7.74%→8.94%). WPI at 9.92% YoY (prev 9.78%), at 70th percentile. Brent crude at $89.7/bbl (flat), WTI at $83.2/bbl (flat), but FAO food index at 136 (up from 128.5 five months ago).","implication":"RBI's inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY is now at risk — headline CPI at 6.09% is 99 bps above target. Expect RBI to hold rates at 5.25% p.a. for longer (current pause justified). If fuel inflation stays above 20% YoY for two more months, RBI may signal a rate hike in Q2 FY2027. Reduce duration exposure in fixed income; overweight floating-rate bonds. For equities, avoid consumer staples (margin compression from input cost inflation); overweight energy and fertiliser stocks (beneficiaries of high commodity prices).","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a structural risk — it typically precedes broader CPI acceleration and forces central banks to tighten. The last time fuel inflation was this high (2022), RBI raised rates by 190 bps over six months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"Fed Tightening Resumes; BOJ Shock Looms","data_text":"Fed funds rate at 3.88% p.a. (prev 3.75%), up from 3.63% three months ago — rising three months in a row (3.63%→3.63%→3.75%→3.88%). US CPI at 3.72% YoY (prev 3.35%), rising three months straight (2.4%→3.3%→3.35%→3.72%). US core PCE at 3.12% YoY (prev 3.03%), up from 3.01% two months ago. US GDP at 3.4% SAAR (prev 2.2%), rising three months straight (0.7%→1.5%→2.2%→3.4%). BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (prev 1%), at 100th percentile of 10-year range — a shock hike. ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (prev 2.25%), rising two months in a row. US 10-year Treasury yield at 5.04% (down from 5.07% prior month, but at 91st percentile).","implication":"Global liquidity is tightening. The Fed is re-tightening (not cutting as markets expected), and the BOJ's shock hike signals a regime shift in carry-trade funding. This is a headwind for EM equities and INR. Reduce leverage; increase cash allocation. For India, expect FII outflows to persist (FII equity net at -₹4,516 cr / month latest). Overweight INR hedges (long USD, short INR). The US 10-year yield at 5.04% is a ceiling for Indian bond yields — expect 10-year GSec yields to stay above 6.5% p.a.","pct_10y":91,"pct_note":"US 10-year Treasury yield at 91st percentile is historically associated with EM capital flight and currency depreciation. The last time yields were this high (2023), INR weakened 8% in three months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"watch","title":"INR Weakens as Carry Unwinds; RBI Intervening","data_text":"INR at 92.59 ₹/USD (prev 92.66 ₹), down from 93.46 ₹/USD five months ago — a 87 paise depreciation over five months. DXY at 103.77 (at 60th percentile), up from 103.4 five months ago. FII equity net at -₹4,516 cr / month (latest), down from +₹29,631 cr / month three months ago — a sharp reversal. DII equity net at ₹6,222 cr / month (latest), down from ₹58,502 cr / month three months ago. India VIX at 17.32 (at 51st percentile), up from 15.41 three months ago. US VIX at 35.89 (at 62nd percentile), up from 19.3 five months ago.","implication":"RBI is intervening to support INR (evident from the modest depreciation despite sharp FII outflows). However, if BOJ carry unwinds accelerate, INR could weaken to 94-95 ₹/USD in the next 2-3 months. Hedge INR exposure; reduce long USD positions (they're crowded). For equity portfolios, reduce IT services exposure (earnings in USD, but valuations compress when INR weakens). Overweight exporters (auto, pharma, chemicals) — they benefit from INR weakness. Monitor RBI's FX reserve adequacy; if reserves fall below $600 bn, RBI may tighten liquidity further.","pct_10y":60,"pct_note":"DXY at 60th percentile is not extreme, but the trend is up. INR weakness is typically a lagging indicator of EM stress — it follows equity outflows by 2-4 weeks.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Pullback","data_text":"Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (latest), down from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter five months ago — a 79% collapse in one quarter. This is at 0th percentile of 10-year range (data only available for ~2 years, but this is a structural break). Office vacancy at 13.4% (down from 14.8% five months ago, but the absorption data shows this is a lagging indicator). Nifty IT index flat at 25,800 (at 87th percentile), but IT services credit growth at 28.3% YoY (rising three months: 21.4%→22.9%→24.3%→28.3%). Contrast: IT credit is accelerating, but office absorption is collapsing. This divergence is the signal.","implication":"Global Capability Centers (GCCs) are the marginal buyer of office space, not traditional IT services firms. The collapse in absorption suggests GCCs are pulling back on expansion — a leading indicator of IT services demand weakness in 2-3 quarters. This is NOT reflected in current IT credit growth (which is driven by legacy IT services firms still hiring). Reduce IT services exposure; overweight IT hardware/semiconductor plays (less exposed to GCC pullback). The office market is decoupling from the IT stock proxy — commercial RE REITs (Embassy, Mindspace, Brookfield) are down 12-18% YTD, and this weakness will persist. Falsifiable: if office absorption rebounds to > 10 mn sq ft / quarter in the next two quarters, GCC pullback is temporary.","pct_10y":0,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 0th percentile is a structural break. Historically, absorption below 5 mn sq ft / quarter preceded IT services revenue growth slowdowns by 2-3 quarters. This is a non-consensus signal.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

Services Carry the Headline — Goods Economy Lags Behind

The facts:

  • GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI Composite at 56.5 signal broad expansion, with manufacturing (55.7) and services (55.8) both above 50.
  • IIP Capital Goods at 16.9% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — both rising two months running — confirm the investment cycle is real.
  • But core sector growth decelerated to 4.8% YoY (from 5.0% prior month), and GST at ₹2,31,290 cr / month includes a 23% month-on-month jump that may reflect advance filings, not pure demand.
  • Household debt at 47.8% of GDP (up from 45.5%) signals consumption is increasingly debt-funded — a structural fragility beneath the headline.

The tension: The investment cycle (capex goods, utilisation) and services PMI are genuine; the goods economy and informal sector are not keeping pace, and the GST record needs triangulation against e-way bill volumes before it earns its headline.

Bottom line: Watch core sector growth: a second consecutive month below 5.0% YoY would confirm the goods economy is decoupling from the investment headline.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Re-Accelerates, BOJ Shocks — EM Carry Trade in the Crossfire

The facts:

  • US GDP at 3.4% SAAR (rising three months: 0.7%→1.5%→2.2%→3.4%) with US PMI Composite at 58.4 — the strongest DM growth print in this cycle.
  • But US CPI at 3.72% YoY (rising three months straight) and Core PCE at 3.12% YoY mean the Fed at 3.88% p.a. is not done — the market is underpricing the terminal rate.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. — a 100th-percentile shock hike — is unwinding yen carry trades that funded EM positioning; US VIX at 35.89 (up from 19.3 five months ago) is the stress gauge.
  • Euro Stoxx 50 at 5,942 has fallen five sessions in a row; S&P 500 at 6,910 has fallen five sessions in a row — DM equity is repricing the rate path, not celebrating the growth.

The tension: US growth is re-accelerating on hard data, but equity markets are falling — because the bond market (US 10Y at 5.04% yield, 91st percentile) is tightening financial conditions faster than the growth data can justify optimism.

Bottom line: BOJ is the underappreciated tail risk: each 25 bps hike unwinds carry trades that have funded India FII positioning — watch the next BOJ meeting for a second consecutive hike.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

SIP Autopilot Holds — But Institutional Conviction Is Fading

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,160 cr / month (94th percentile) remain structurally elevated, but SIP YoY growth has decelerated sharply to 8.9% YoY from 19.85% five months ago.
  • Equity MF net inflows fell to ₹32,994 cr / month from ₹38,307 cr / month prior month — a ₹5,313 cr / month drop in a single period.
  • FII equity net at -₹4,516 cr / month, reversed from +₹29,631 cr / month three months ago; DII net at ₹6,222 cr / month, down from ₹58,502 cr / month — both sides of the institutional bid are shrinking.
  • But MF AUM at ₹83.39 lakh cr (86th percentile) is holding, supported by mark-to-market on a Nifty that has risen four of the last five sessions.

The tension: Retail SIP flows are the floor, but the institutional bid — both FII and DII — has contracted sharply; if SIP growth continues decelerating toward single digits, the floor itself becomes a question.

Bottom line: Watch equity MF net inflows: a print below ₹28,000 cr / month would signal retail conviction is following institutional money out the door.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Bank Nifty at All-Time High, REITs at Multi-Year Lows — Pricing Opposite Realities

The facts:

  • NRI buying is falling — NRI share of residential purchases at 18% (down 2 pp from prior print), with NRI share within premium/luxury at 32%; remittances at $155.1 bn (14.5% YoY) are holding but not translating into property purchases.
  • Hyderabad leads residential momentum: sales +15% YoY, launches +120% YoY, price +6% YoY, 28 months unsold inventory — the launch surge risks a supply overhang within 6 quarters.
  • Bank Nifty at 64,635 (100th percentile) is pricing a banking system with pristine funding; Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, Brookfield at ₹263/unit — all down 12–31% from prior prints — are pricing office demand destruction.
  • Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (0th percentile, down from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter five months ago) with GCCs at 42% of occupier mix — if GCC leasing has paused, the REIT income thesis breaks.

The tension: Bank Nifty at an all-time high assumes credit growth sustains without funding stress; REIT prices at multi-year lows assume office absorption has structurally broken. Both cannot be right simultaneously — one is mispriced.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until Q4 2026 absorption data confirms whether the 79% quarterly collapse is a one-quarter anomaly or a GCC structural pullback.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Three Fuses, One Detonator — Inflation, Carry, and Credit

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, up 288 bps in one month) with Brent at $89.7/bbl flat — any crude spike above $95/bbl pushes headline CPI to 6.5%+ YoY and forces RBI's hand.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) unwinding carry trades: FII equity net already at -₹4,516 cr / month; a second BOJ hike could accelerate outflows and test INR at 94–95.
  • CD ratio at 82% (75th percentile) with services credit at 28.3% YoY — if deposit growth slips below 15% YoY, the regulator's macro-prudential toolkit (risk weight hikes on unsecured lending) gets activated within one quarter.
  • But S&P 500 falling five sessions in a row to 6,910 with US VIX at 35.89 — a global risk-off that deepens could compress India's equity risk premium and trigger passive EM outflows regardless of domestic fundamentals.

The tension: Each risk is individually manageable; the danger is sequencing — a BOJ hike triggers carry unwind, FII outflows weaken INR, imported fuel inflation accelerates, RBI is forced to hike into a credit system already running on thin deposit cover.

Bottom line: Watch India CPI (next release): a print above 6.3% YoY would make an RBI rate hike within two meetings near-certain and reprice the entire rate-sensitive complex.

"}
